title: 2 Kings 24:18–20
context: Zedekiah, twenty-one years old, reigns eleven years and does evil like Jehoiakim. The narrator explains that this happened through the anger of the LORD until he cast them out of his presence, and then Zedekiah rebels against Babylon. Both traditions read this as shared ground about judgment already announced, and the same notice appears in Jeremiah 52:1–3.

verses.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note that his mother, Hamutal, was also the mother of Jehoahaz (cf. 23:31).

Jeremiah 52:1 gives the same notice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the last king of Judah introduced in the same pattern as his predecessors.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the narrator presents Zedekiah’s reign as the final chapter of the kingdom.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.” Arminian readers note that Zedekiah, though placed on the throne by Babylon, is responsible for his own choices.

Jeremiah records his repeated reluctance to heed the prophet’s counsel (cf. Jer 38:14–23).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same verdict that marked his brother’s reign.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the king’s evil is real and his own, and it continues the pattern that led to judgment.

verses.text: For through the anger of the LORD, this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until he had cast them out from his presence. Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For through the anger of the LORD, this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until he had cast them out from his presence. Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.” Arminian readers note that the narrator places human rebellion within God’s judgment.

Zedekiah’s choice is real and has consequences.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the LORD’s anger as the governing cause of the events, with Zedekiah’s rebellion as the means.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the judgment had been announced, Zedekiah is responsible for his rebellion, and God is just in what follows.
